questions.enonce_markdown:
With the use of diagram(s) distinguish between a Progressive Tax System and a Regressive Tax System.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Progressive tax system.** A tax system in which the *proportion* of income taken in tax **rises as income rises**: the rich pay a higher percentage of their income than the poor. Income tax with higher rates on higher bands of income is an example. It follows the *ability-to-pay* principle and reduces inequality.

**Regressive tax system.** A tax system in which the *proportion* of income taken in tax **falls as income rises**: the poor pay a higher percentage of their income than the rich. A tax of the same amount on every person (a poll or flat-sum tax), or a tax on basic goods that poor people spend most of their income on, is an example. It increases inequality.

*Numerical illustration (hypothetical figures).*

| Income (FCFA) | Progressive: tax paid | Rate | Regressive (flat sum 10,000 FCFA): tax paid | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 | 5,000 | 5% | 10,000 | 10% |
| 200,000 | 20,000 | 10% | 10,000 | 5% |
| 400,000 | 80,000 | 20% | 10,000 | 2.5% |

![fig-1](gce-ol-economics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_8_fig_1.png)

**Reading the diagrams.** In both diagrams the horizontal axis shows income and the vertical axis shows the tax paid as a percentage of income (the average tax rate). In diagram (a) the curve **slopes upward**: the higher the income, the higher the average tax rate (progressive). In diagram (b) the curve **slopes downward**: the higher the income, the lower the average tax rate (regressive). The dashed horizontal line is a *proportional* tax, where the rate is the same at every income.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain Five (05) criteria any Government takes into account, in introducing a new form of tax.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A good tax should satisfy certain principles (the *canons of taxation*, first set out by Adam Smith and later extended). A government takes these into account when it introduces a new tax.

1. **Equity (fairness).** The tax should be fair, related to each person's ability to pay: people with higher incomes or wealth should pay more, and people in the same situation should be treated alike. A tax that is felt to be unfair is resisted and evaded.
2. **Certainty.** Taxpayers should know clearly how much they must pay, when and how. The tax should not be arbitrary, so that people can plan their affairs and tax collectors cannot abuse their power.
3. **Convenience.** The tax should be paid at a time and in a way convenient to the taxpayer, for example income tax deducted from the salary each month or VAT included in the price when buying.
4. **Economy.** The cost of collecting the tax should be small compared with the revenue it brings. A tax that costs almost as much to collect as it yields is a waste.
5. **Productivity (adequate yield).** The tax should raise enough revenue for the government's needs, and a tax on goods with a wide base (many buyers) is better than one that brings in little.

*Other acceptable criteria:* flexibility (the rate can be changed easily as needs change), effects on incentives to work, save and invest, and difficulty of evasion.

**Conclusion.** A government that applies these criteria obtains the revenue it needs without too much cost or injustice.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain any Two (02) reasons why a Government may adopt a budget deficit

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A *budget deficit* occurs when government spending is greater than government revenue in a year. A government may deliberately adopt it for the following reasons.

1. **To stimulate the economy and reduce unemployment.** In a recession or a period of high unemployment, the government spends more than it collects in taxes (or cuts taxes). This increases total demand, output and employment.
2. **To finance development projects.** Spending on roads, schools, hospitals, energy and other capital projects is large, and it benefits future generations too. The government may borrow to pay for them, since the projects increase the productive capacity of the economy.

*Other acceptable reasons:* to meet emergencies such as floods, epidemics or war, and because spending on unemployment and social benefits rises automatically when incomes fall.
